blogDescription: A concise neighborhood-by-neighborhood look at where single-family homes and condos stand across the Portland metro. Highlights the most competitive pockets, where buyers have more room to negotiate, and what to expect if you're buying or selling right now.
blogIntroduction:
Across Greater Portland the single-family market and the condo market are behaving quite differently. For single-family homes the metro-level picture shows about 2.5 months of inventory, a pending-to-active ratio around 28%, and homes that sold in about 43 days on average. That mix points to relatively tighter supply and quicker sales for detached homes overall. Condominiums, by contrast, are sitting with roughly 6.9 months of inventory, a lower pending-to-active ratio, and longer marketing times, so buyers generally face more choices and more time to decide when looking at condos.

Within the metro there are big local differences. Some neighborhoods are moving very quickly, particularly several inner-Portland areas for single-family homes, while other counties and many condo submarkets show higher inventory and longer days on market. That means strategy should be neighborhood- and property-type specific rather than metro-wide.
competitiveMarketsIntro: The single-family pockets with the least supply and the quickest sales right now include Northeast Portland (about 1.5 months of inventory, average days on market about 28), North Portland (1.6 months, roughly 29 days), and Southeast Portland (1.9 months, about 28 days). Low months of inventory combined with strong pending activity and short days on market generally indicates these listings move fast and buyers have less time to shop around.
buyerOpportunityIntro: If you want more negotiating room and extra time to evaluate homes, look at the areas with higher months of inventory and longer marketing times. Columbia County (4.4 months of inventory, average days on market about 73), Yamhill County (4.2 months, about 62 days) and Marion County (4.2 months, about 54 days) are showing the kind of supply and marketing time that tend to create more flexibility for buyers on price and terms.
condoMarketIntro: Condos are acting differently from detached homes in many parts of the metro. Several condo markets have months of inventory in the mid-to-high single digits, and some neighborhoods are well into double-digit days on market. That suggests more choices and generally slower-moving listings for condo shoppers compared with single-family buyers in the same neighborhoods.
condoComparisonAnalysis: Look at the contrasts in the same neighborhoods. In North Portland single-family inventory is about 1.6 months while condos sit at roughly 9.8 months, and single-family homes sold in about 29 days versus condos at about 112 days. In Northeast Portland the gap is similar: single-family around 1.5 months and 28 days, condos about 6.3 months and 113 days. Even in Lake Oswego/West Linn single-family homes move faster (about 3.8 months, roughly 37 days) than condos there (about 9.3 months, roughly 84 days). In short, in many neighborhoods single-family listings are faster-moving and tighter, condos offer more inventory and more time to decide.
buyerTakeaways: If you’re shopping for a single-family home in Northeast, North or Southeast Portland expect a short decision window — listings there are often under 30 days from listing to sale.
Condo buyers, especially in North Portland and Lake Oswego, should plan for a longer search and more options: you’ll usually have more time to compare units and negotiate.
In higher-inventory counties like Columbia and Yamhill you may find more flexibility on price and terms, and more time for inspections and contingencies.
Get financing and inspections aligned early when pursuing faster-moving single-family listings so you can act quickly without compromising due diligence.
sellerTakeaways: Sellers of single-family homes in tight pockets (NE, North, SE Portland) should prepare for faster marketing timelines: professional prep and clear pricing help capture buyer interest quickly.
Condo sellers should budget for longer marketing periods and more competition — pricing and presentation matter because buyers have more choices.
If you’re selling in higher-inventory counties, be realistic on timing and the potential need to highlight value through updates or stronger marketing.
Work with your agent to set a timeline that matches your neighborhood and property type so you’re ready for either a quick sale or a longer marketing period.
closing: Portland is not one housing market — it’s dozens. Buyers and sellers should focus on the specific neighborhood, property type and price range that matters to them, because the difference between a fast-moving single-family market and a slower condo market can be dramatic.
reelScript: Single-family homes are selling a lot faster than condos across the metro — about 2.5 months of inventory for houses versus roughly 6.9 months for condos.
